I am 71 years old, and my back tells me the weather before the radio does. Fifty years on this same patch of Quzhou soil has taught me not to get greedy. My wife and I are the only two left in our household, so every mu must earn its keep without breaking our backs.

All 10.5 mu are already in wheat. I sowed it last October with an improved variety I have trusted for years, because wheat is the backbone of our food — without it, we have no flour for our steamed buns and noodles. This spring, I will top-dress it once and irrigate it twice more before the June harvest. After the wheat comes off, I will split the land: 7 mu will go to millet and 3.5 mu to maize. Millet is hardy, drinks less water than maize, and I have grown it my whole life; it fills our own grain jars and the market price has been steady. The maize will be hybrid seed from the shop in town — expensive, but the heavy ears bring in cash and feed. I will use the rotary tiller for both summer crops because I no longer have the strength to handle a plough like I did at thirty. I will give the millet one good irrigation and modest fertilizer; it has deep roots and I do not waste my well water. The maize will get two irrigations and a bit more feed, and I will watch it for the corn borer. I do not blanket my fields with chemicals — two sprays for wheat, one for millet, and two for maize is enough. My goal is to fill our own stores first; whatever is left goes to market.
